trial_name: ALPS — Amiodarone, Lidocaine, or Placebo in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (2016)
citation: Kudenchuk PJ, Brown SP, Daya M, et al. Amiodarone, lidocaine, or placebo in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(18):1711-1722.
trial_type: RCT — multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, prehospital, parallel-group
one_liner: In shock-refractory VF/pVT OHCA, amiodarone and lidocaine improve admission outcomes but do not clearly improve overall discharge survival; any survival signal is most apparent in witnessed arrests.

pico.population: Adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT after at least one shock, with IV/IO access
pico.intervention: Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO (plus optional 150 mg) or lidocaine 120 mg IV/IO (plus optional 60 mg)
pico.outcome: Survival to hospital discharge (primary); functionally favourable survival (mRS ≤3) at discharge

background.existing_knowledge: Antiarrhythmic drugs (notably amiodarone, and historically lidocaine) were incorporated into resuscitation algorithms for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT largely on the basis of modest prehospital trials demonstrating improved short-term endpoints (e.g., survival to hospital admission), with persistent uncertainty about patient-centred outcomes (survival with good neurological function).
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty about patient-centred outcomes (survival with good neurological function).
background.hypothesis: In adults with OHCA and shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT, treatment with amiodarone or lidocaine (vs placebo) improves survival to hospital discharge, and amiodarone is superior to lidocaine.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, prehospital, parallel-group (1:1:1), Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (ROC); conducted under exception from informed consent.
methods.setting: EMS-treated OHCA in ROC catchment (10 North American ROC centres; >200 EMS agencies; >250 receiving hospitals).

inclusion: Adults with OHCA and persistent/recurrent VF or pulseless VT after at least one shock, with IV/IO access and an indication for antiarrhythmic therapy.
exclusion: Traumatic arrest; DNR/“opt out”; known pregnancy/prisoner; known allergy to study drugs; receipt of an antiarrhythmic before randomisation; non-shockable rhythms at the time of intended dosing (handled via post-randomisation exclusion from the per-protocol “efficacy” population).

methods.intervention: Amiodarone (PM101 formulation): 150 mg per syringe; initial dose 300 mg (2 syringes) after shock-refractory VF/pVT, with an additional 150 mg (1 syringe) if VF/pVT persisted/recured (maximum 450 mg). Lidocaine: 60 mg per syringe; initial dose 120 mg (2 syringes), with an additional 60 mg (1 syringe) if VF/pVT persisted/recured (maximum 180 mg).
methods.comparison: Placebo (normal saline), visually identical syringes and dosing schedule to maintain blinding.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (EMS clinicians, in-hospital clinicians, investigators, and outcome assessors blinded); emergency unblinding permitted via prespecified process (infrequent).
methods.sample_size_power: A target of 3000 patients in the per-protocol (“efficacy”) population provided 90% power to detect an absolute increase in survival to discharge from 23.4% to 29.7%; group-sequential design with one-sided significance level 0.025 for each active drug vs placebo and two-sided 0.05 for amiodarone vs lidocaine.
secondary_outcomes: Functionally favourable survival at discharge (Modified Rankin Scale ≤3)

headline_bullets: Neither amiodarone nor lidocaine significantly improved survival to hospital discharge vs placebo in the primary per-protocol analysis.
Both drugs significantly improved hospital admission rates (amiodarone +5.8%, lidocaine +7.4% vs placebo).
In witnessed arrests, both drugs showed ~5% absolute improvement in discharge survival (interaction P=0.05).
Intention-to-treat analyses showed smaller, non-significant differences in discharge survival.

outcomes_table.note: Adjusted CI/P for sequential monitoring; per-protocol primary analysis.
No statistically significant difference vs placebo at prespecified boundary.
No evidence of superiority of amiodarone over lidocaine.
mRS unavailable in a small number; denominators reflect available mRS.
Intermediate endpoint; not powered for mechanistic outcomes.
Signal for improved short-term physiology without clear translation to discharge survival.
Consistent with an effect on early resuscitation success.
Largest observed difference among intermediate outcomes.
Interpretation limited by ascertainment during post-arrest care.
Consistent with bradyarrhythmic effects; other serious adverse events were uncommon.

subgroup_table.group_a: Amiodarone or Lidocaine (combined analysis not fully reported)
subgroup_table.note: Approximate absolute improvement; interaction P=0.05 for witnessed vs unwitnessed; exact subgroup counts not provided in main paper.

safety: Lidocaine associated with higher clinical seizure activity within 24 hours (5.1% vs 3.7%, P=0.05).
Amiodarone associated with higher temporary cardiac pacing within 24 hours (4.9% vs 2.7%, P=0.006).
Other serious adverse events were uncommon and similar between groups.

domains.notes: Allocation occurred via opening a blinded trial-drug kit with central randomisation; concealment and blinding were strong by design (prehospital environment, identical syringes).
Double-blind design mitigated differential co-interventions; unblinding was rare (24/3026, 0.8%).

4667 randomised; 4653 included in intention-to-treat; 3026 included in the per-protocol population; primary endpoint analysis used 970 (amiodarone), 985 (lidocaine), 1056 (placebo), after additional small exclusions for missing outcome data (4 in per-protocol). This large post-randomisation attrition from the primary analysis set is a major threat to strict ITT inference.

Time from 911 call to first dose was similar (amiodarone 19.3±7.4 min vs lidocaine 19.3±7.4 min vs placebo 19.3±7.2 min); shocks after first dose were also similar (3.6±4.8 vs 3.4±4.5 vs 3.5±4.6), supporting comparable exposure windows. Open-label antiarrhythmic use was low but numerically higher in placebo (amiodarone 1.4% and lidocaine 1.2% in placebo vs ≤1.3% in active arms), reducing risk of major “contamination”.

Per-protocol groups were well balanced: mean age 63.5±13.6 vs 63.5±13.8 vs 63.3±13.6 years; men 77.9% vs 77.5% vs 78.9%; bystander witnessed 58.4% vs 57.6% vs 58.8%; bystander CPR 56.8% vs 57.9% vs 59.5%; time from call to EMS arrival 5.0±2.7 vs 5.1±2.9 vs 5.0±2.7 min.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate—randomisation, blinding, and baseline balance were strong, but reliance on a per-protocol primary analysis with substantial post-randomisation exclusions limits the robustness of causal inference for the trial’s primary estimand.

domains.notes: Reflects adult OHCA with shock-refractory VF/pVT managed by advanced EMS systems capable of IV/IO access, defibrillation, and protocolised ALS; excludes non-shockable rhythms and trauma.

Applicability is highest in systems resembling ROC (high-quality CPR/defibrillation infrastructure, transport and post-arrest care capacity); generalisability is reduced where drug delivery is delayed, vascular access is not feasible, or post-arrest care differs substantially. Amiodarone formulation (PM101) and dose schedule were aligned with contemporary ALS practice, but formulation differences may matter in other settings.

external_validity.verdict: Good for shock-refractory VF/pVT OHCA in well-developed EMS systems; limited for non-shockable arrests and for systems without timely drug delivery or comparable post-arrest pathways.

strengths: Pragmatic prehospital implementation within a mature research network.
Clinically important primary endpoint (survival to discharge) with functional outcome captured.
limitations: Primary reliance on a per-protocol (“efficacy”) population with extensive post-randomisation exclusions.
Drug administration occurred relatively late in the resuscitation timeline (mean ~19 minutes from 911 call), potentially diluting effect.
Hospital and post-arrest care not protocolised (pragmatic but introduces downstream variability).
Three-arm comparisons with multiple secondary endpoints increase interpretive complexity.

critical_appraisal.summary: ALPS was a large, well-conducted RCT with strong internal validity for its per-protocol analysis, but the primary reliance on per-protocol population and late drug administration limit confidence in overall effect on discharge survival. The trial provides moderate-quality evidence that antiarrhythmics improve early resuscitation endpoints but not discharge survival overall, with a possible benefit in witnessed arrests.
weaknesses: Per-protocol primary analysis with substantial post-randomisation exclusions
Late drug administration (~19 min) may dilute effect
Multiple secondary endpoints increase risk of false positives

sections.authors_conclusion: Antiarrhythmic drugs improve intermediate outcomes (hospital admission) but do not clearly improve survival to discharge overall. A potential benefit exists in witnessed arrests, where absolute improvements of ~5% were observed, suggesting time-dependent efficacy.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not change routine practice; antiarrhythmics remain reasonable options for shock-refractory VF/pVT, but emphasis should remain on rapid defibrillation and high-quality CPR. Consider use particularly in witnessed arrests where benefit may be greater.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT in EMS systems with timely drug delivery.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That antiarrhythmics are ineffective; they improve early resuscitation success, but this does not consistently translate to discharge survival.
implementation_caveats: Drug administration should not delay defibrillation or CPR.
Benefit likely time-dependent; greatest in witnessed arrests with short downtime.
Formulation and dosing may vary; this trial used specific formulations (PM101 amiodarone).

controversies.notes: The trial’s principal causal estimate was anchored to a post-randomisation “efficacy/per-protocol” population, which risks bias if exclusions relate to prognosis or are influenced by early resuscitation dynamics; this design choice drove post-publication critique.

Both active drugs improved admission to hospital, but the effect attenuated by discharge—raising questions about drug timing, post-arrest brain injury dominating prognosis, and downstream care variability.
The witnessed-arrest interaction (P=0.05) is clinically coherent but near the conventional threshold; must be interpreted in context of multiple subgroup tests and modest absolute effect sizes.

Post-ALPS systematic reviews and network meta-analyses generally support improved ROSC/survival to hospital admission with amiodarone/lidocaine, with inconsistent or modest effects on survival to discharge and neurological outcomes, mirroring ALPS’ pattern of results.

Subsequent guideline statements continue to endorse either amiodarone or lidocaine as reasonable therapies for shock-refractory VF/pVT, while emphasising that the certainty for improvement in patient-centred outcomes remains limited.

context_related_trials.trial: Post-ALPS systematic reviews and network meta-analyses
context_related_trials.relation: These analyses pooled ALPS with earlier trials, showing consistent improvement in ROSC and hospital admission with amiodarone/lidocaine, but inconsistent effects on survival to discharge and neurological outcomes.

unresolved_questions: Does earlier drug administration (e.g., after first shock) improve discharge survival?
Can post-arrest care protocols enhance translation of early ROSC benefit to long-term survival?
Is there a subgroup (e.g., shorter downtime) that derives clear mortality benefit?
What is the optimal antiarrhythmic agent and dosing in the current era of high-quality CPR?

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome: survival to discharge 24.4% amiodarone vs 21.0% placebo (risk diff +3.2%, P=0.08)
Lidocaine vs placebo: 23.7% vs 21.0% (risk diff +2.6%, P=0.16)
Hospital admission: amiodarone +5.8%, lidocaine +7.4% vs placebo (both significant)
Witnessed arrest subgroup: ~5% absolute improvement in discharge survival (interaction P=0.05)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In shock-refractory VF/pVT, amiodarone or lidocaine may improve early resuscitation success but do not clearly increase survival to discharge; consider use in witnessed arrests where benefit is plausible.
